newsitem.title: Pakistan: FOCUS-IMF to discuss new loan to Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-IMF to discuss new loan to Pakistan.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund has agreed to negotiate a new structural adjustment loan to Pakistan after suspending the current standby arrangement, Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz said on Friday.

He said an economic reform package to be announced by new Prime Minister Nawaz Shari soon would form the basis for talks later this year for a softer medium-term extended structural adjustment facility (ESAF) or an extended fund facility (EFF).

An IMF mission, reviewing Pakistan's economic performance before deciding whether to recommend the release this month of the next $122 million standby tranche, left Islamabad on Friday after two weeks of talks without making any public statement.
Aziz said Sharif's government, voted into power in February 3 elections, would unveil an industrial revival package in the next few days and an agricultural revival package on April 3.
"We will supplement the demand side measures with supply side measures," he said. "This we hope will give a major boost to our economy."
Asked if the standby loan had been suspended, Aziz said: "You can say it has been suspended till this (new) programme gets going."

The IMF resumed the loan in December after a caretaker government promised to cut the budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product in 1996/97 (July-June) from 6.3 percent in 1995/96, but officials say the target cannot be met by June.

Aziz said the mission's evaluation up to December was "generally in line with the standby targets" but the figures for January and February were deficient on the revenue side and on the overall performance because of elections and other factors.
But he said the IMF officials had been told that pursuing only those targets would not serve the purpose. "The more important priority for us is to revive the economy," he said.
"The mission welcomed the government's intention to move forward on a bold programme of structural reform," a government statement released at Aziz's news conference said.

"It endorses the government's desire to move decisively to take radical measures for the reform of taxes and of tax administration as well as for accelerated privatisation and the revival of the industrial and agricultural sectors.
"The government's policy package, when implemented fully, will lay the basis for a transition to negotiations of a medium-term ESAF/EFF arrangement," it said.
"It was decided that negotiations for the new arrangement could commence immediately after successful implementation of these policies."
Aziz said Pakistan's programme would get IMF support if the fund liked it. "This is how it should be," he added.

"We should not be implementing the fund's programme here at their priority. We should implement priorities which are in our national interest and our priorities, and if the fund wants to support it, they are welcome to do so," he said.
"So the nature of the relationship is changing from a fund-driven programme to a Pakistan-driven programme."
